https://www.dw.com/en/russia-opens-first.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M4bT The new Russia-North Korea road bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Russia and North Korea on Monday cut the ribbon on the first road bridge linking the two countries as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen their strategic partnership. The crossing spans the Tumen River and marks another expansion of transport links between the two countries. Where is the new bridge? The road crossing is near the existing Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge commissioned in 1959 following the Korean War. Russia and North Korea already have direct rail and air connections, but until now there had been no road bridge between them. The new bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life. Relatives of Novichenko attended the opening ceremony. Nikolai Shcherbitsky and Tatyana Shcherbitskaya joined the ceremony to unveil the bridge named after their grandfather and father respectively Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance Construction began in April 2025 after the project was agreed during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024. Why is the road bridge being opened now? Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the new crossing should boost economic development, tourism and employment. "I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," the TASS news agency quoted Mishustin as saying by video link at the opening ceremony. Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened considerably since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion launched in 2024. https://www.rferl.org/a/us-senator-jeann.text: Accessibility links Skip to main content Skip to main Navigation Skip to Search Print Options: Images Multimedia Embedded Content Comments Russia US Senator Jeanne Shaheen: 'Putin Is Trying To Wait Us Out' By Alex Raufoglu September 17, 2026 23:34 CET US Senator Jeanne Shaheen: 'Putin Is Trying To Wait Us Out' Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Senator Jeanne Shaheen talks to the press during a visit to Chisinau early this year. (file photo) WASHINGTON -- With a sweeping Russia sanctions bill headed to President Donald Trump's desk, US Senator Jeanne Shaheen told RFE/RL the legislation is intended to squeeze Moscow's energy revenues and pressure countries buying Russian oil and gas. She also discussed in an interview with RFE/RL on September 17 Ukraine's urgent military needs, the prospects for diplomacy, Russian hybrid warfare, and security risks in the Balkans. RFE/RL: Congress has just passed the Russia sanctions bill, the first major bipartisan congressional legislation supporting Ukraine since the emergency aid package approved in April 2024. What changes for Moscow now that the legislation is headed to Trump's desk? Jeanne Shaheen: Hopefully it sends an important message. It was a very strong bipartisan vote in both houses. In the Senate, it passed 86 to 11, and it passed with over 100 votes yesterday in the House with overwhelming bipartisan support. [Editor's note: The House passed the bill 262-159 on September 16.] Both Democrats and Republicans supported it. What it would do is crack down not just on Russia's financial industry, the oligarchs, and those people around Vladimir Putin who are helping to make this war possible for Russia. It would also crack down on the revenue that's funding this war -- the oil and gas revenue. Embed share US Senator Shaheen: China Will Feel Impact Of Russia Sanctions by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:05 0:00 Direct link 240p | 1.4MB 360p | 1.8MB 480p | 2.6MB 720p | 3.9MB 1080p | 6.4MB It would tariff the top five countries that are using Russian oil and gas, and that's really China and India. They're the big users. And what we've heard from India is that if this bill passed, they were going to stop buying Russian oil and gas. [Editor's note: The legislation authorizes tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas, subject to certain exceptions.] So hopefully it will send a strong message not just to Putin and Russia but to China and those other purchasers of Russian oil and gas. It shuts down the shadow fleet [vessels used to evade restrictions on its oil trade]. But also, to Ukraine, we had a press conference yesterday where the leaders in both houses talked about the message to the Ukrainians. It is to tell them we appreciate their courage. They're fighting for democracy and freedom, and we're going to try and do everything we can to support them. RFE/RL: How quickly could these sanctions begin putting measurable pressure on Russia's war economy, and what will determine how fast they take effect? Shaheen: That depends on the administration. Now, the president is planning to sign this bill within the next day or so. Hopefully, as soon as it's signed, we'll see the Treasury Department begin to put those sanctions in place. We worked very closely with the trade representative, Ambassador Jamieson Greer, on the legislation, so that they are engaged in it and they're looking at the countries and how to determine which of those countries are affected. So we're very hopeful that we're going to see action by the administration as soon as the bill passes. RFE/RL: Critics have questioned whether the sanctions will actually alter Moscow's calculations. What specific indicators will you be watching in the weeks and months ahead to determine whether the measures are working? Shaheen: We're going to be watching the implementation very closely. It's not just the sanctions piece that we think is important, but it's also, as I said, shutting down the revenues. Russia gets over 50 percent of its revenue from selling oil and gas. And we know that Europe's already weaned itself off of Russian oil and is in the process of weaning itself off of Russian gas. But there are other countries in the world that have not done that. SEE ALSO: US Congress Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It To Trump Most notably, China. China needs to get the message that if they want to continue to buy Russian gas, if they want to continue to help Russia fuel and pay for this unprovoked war that is killing civilians, that is horrific, and that Russia is losing about 35,000 Russian soldiers a month in casualties, then they're going to have to pay. And they're going to have to pay market value. No more of this getting oil and gas on the black market through the shadow fleet, where they're not paying market prices. RFE/RL: Ukraine is entering another difficult phase of the war. You are in regular contact with Ukrainian officials. What does Kyiv most urgently need from Washington right now? Shaheen: We need to do everything we can to provide those interceptors that are helping them defend against the Russian missiles. That is a challenge because we are having difficulties with our defense industrial base, not just in the United States, but in our European allies. And I think we're trying to do everything we can to get those interceptors to the country. SEE ALSO: A Quiet Ukrainian Counteroffensive, A 'Rout' For Russian Forces We need to make sure they've got Starlink connections so they can track what's going on with Russian missiles. And we need to help them prepare for what's going to be another very cold winter. We need to think of every way we can to put pressure on Vladimir Putin to get him to the table to stop this war. His economy is teetering at this point. RFE/RL: Trump has talked about an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine. Under what conditions could a limited cease-fire become a pathway toward a broader settlement? Shaheen: It depends on how it's structured and whether Russia is really serious about coming to the table. So far, they haven't been. Vladimir Putin has been stringing everyone along, stringing along the Trump administration and his envoys because he thinks he can wait us out. I think we saw a strong message from Congress in a bipartisan way yesterday that we are not going to let Putin and Russia wait us out. We are going to do everything we can to put pressure on them. RFE/RL: Russia is increasingly using drones, cyberattacks, sabotage, and other tools beyond Ukraine. Where, in your view, does conventional warfare end and hybrid warfare begin? Shaheen: Hybrid warfare has been going on for some time, and we're seeing an increase now. The good news is that the Ukrainians are very innovative. They have stayed ahead of the Russian drone technology, and we need to do everything we can to support that. It's not only in Ukraine's interest; it's in America's interest. What we've seen in the Middle East is that those drones have done significant damage to American assets in the Middle East. We need to be as technologically advanced on drones and counter drones as we can be, and Ukraine can help us with that. SEE ALSO: US, Poland Making Progress On Permanent American Army Base, Trump Says RFE/RL: You have specifically raised concerns about Russian activity along NATO's eastern flank. What, in your assessment, is Moscow testing in the Baltics and in Poland? Shaheen: Well, he's not just testing it in the Baltics. He's testing it in Poland…. We just had a hearing today in the Foreign Relations Committee, and one of the issues that came up was the fact that Serbia has served as a way station for the Russians when they did their attack in Leipzig. They then came back to Serbia. [Editor's note: German authorities are investigating suspected Russian intelligence involvement in an August drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. German media report that a suspect later traveled to Serbia.] We need to make sure we're attacking that hybrid warfare everywhere we can. It's not only in America's interest, but it's in our European allies' interest. RFE/RL: You've raised concerns about the potential for instability involving Kosovo, Serbia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. What concerns you most today? Shaheen: It is the affiliation that Serbia and Serbians in the Republic of Srpska have with Russia and their interest in destabilizing the region. Russia sees that as a potential second front, and we need to do everything we can to maintain stability in the region. And we need to make it clear that our military is also watching very closely. We have a NATO presence in Kosovo. We have the EUFOR mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We need to make sure the Russians know they are on high alert, watching what happens. RFE/RL: Turning to Russia itself, what role can the Russian opposition realistically play while the war continues and repression inside Russia remains intense? Shaheen: They've been very effective in pointing out what's going on in Russia and maintaining ties back to the country in ways that can help increase the dissidents who are on the ground in Russia and sharing information about what Vladimir Putin is doing in terms of cracking down on anybody who doesn't toe the line that he has. SEE ALSO: It's Russia's First Parliamentary Vote Since Invading Ukraine. Don't Expect Surprises. They are revealing the implications for those casualties that are happening. And they're talking about the impact on the Russian economy from the sanctions that have been in place, not only in the United States but in Europe, and also the implications for this new legislation and what that's going to mean. They've been very critical to efforts to hold Putin accountable. RFE/RL: From Ukraine to the Baltics and Poland to the Balkans, are these separate crises, or do you see them as interconnected elements of a broader challenge to European security? Shaheen: Let's be clear. What's happening is all related, and we're seeing Russia collaborate with China, with Iran, with North Korea, not only in Ukraine but Iran. We know the Iranians are using targeting information from China and Russia to help them hit American assets. It is unconscionable that we are not doing everything possible to go after Vladimir Putin, to go after China, to stop their attacks against American men and women who are serving in the Middle East and against our assets there. That's costing American taxpayers money, and it's costing American lives, and it should not be allowed. And this administration needs to do more to shut that down. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/03/uae-.text: The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday. A crash axe is a tool in the cockpit for the pilots to use in an emergency.Prosecutor general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said the co-pilot of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 tried to take control of the aircraft and that the investigation continues “to uncover all the circumstances of the incident, its motives, and related connections, in addition to completing technical examinations and examining physical and digital evidence”, according to UAE state news agency WAM.The co-pilot who nearly crashed the Tel-Aviv bound flight with 182 people aboard is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, according to Associated Press’ sources who also reported, alongside the Wall Street Journal, that he was banned from flying by Oman over concerns that he held radical ideological views.The co-pilot was then hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, a source told the Associated Press. It was not immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted when hired.The co-pilot was born in the UAE and worked with Oman’s national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, officials said. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. Israel says has it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with it. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, according to the AP.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government.The FlyDubai captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar told India’s Prime Ministe Narendra Modhi in an emotional video from his hospital bed in Saudi Arabia on Thursday that he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to come in, subdue the co-pilot and stabilise the plane.Hailed as a global hero for saving the passengers, Machchhar said "I was fighting for my life," adding that "when I was lying on the floor I could feel the aircraft was going down. I knew exactly that this would be the last push. I told myself that if I didn't get up, there would be a problem. I managed to open the door, and then everyone else came in."UAE presidential advisor Anwar Gargash said “the Indian pilot at Flydubai, Smit Machchhar, deserves every bit of appreciation, for he embodied the meaning of courage and responsibility in the face of a dangerous terrorist act and a potential disaster. His professionalism and moral sense in the darkest of circumstances make him a true hero.”“Far from the easy reduction of what happened or the adoption and promotion of conspiracy theories, vigilance and caution remain essential in confronting the risks of extremism and terrorism,“ Gargash added.Amid shock and disbelief within the UAE’s sprawling pilots community, the attack left the region’s travel industry in crisis, raising questions about aviation security and further unsettling a Middle East already shaken by the US-Iran war.The UAE cancelled all flights to Israel, while Israel’s El Al airline cancelled its scheduled flights to the UAE following the incident. Israel and the UAE agreed on repatriation flights to bring back passengers.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/09/six-.text: Heavy rains battered Chile’s capital Santiago and its surrounding regions on Thursday, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, according to authorities.Chilean President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in Las Condes, a wealthy suburb east of Santiago, giving government agencies more power to respond as torrential rains turned key roads into impassable waterways.The district's mayor, Catalina San Martín, said 14.4 centimetres of rain had fallen in recent days — about nine times the average October rainfall — leaving the area “totally drenched.”The Mapocho River, which runs through Santiago, overflowed, prompting evacuation orders.Chile’s disaster-response agency put 10 other districts on high alert for more landslides and ordered schools to close on Friday.Rain storms earlier this week had already damaged a few dozen homes across central Chile and left nearly 12,000 customers in Santiago without power, officials said. The downpours were expected to ease on Friday.No deaths were reported on Thursday as a result of the heavy rains. The injured however included a one-year-old child, who suffered broken bones. Firefighters said they'd rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people.The floods come as a powerful El Niño gains strength.The naturally recurring warming of tropical Pacific waters scrambles rainfall patterns worldwide and often brings wetter springs to the Southern Hemisphere.The World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday that this year’s El Niño was expected to peak in December and could be among the most intense since at least 1950.

https://www.politico.eu/article/valerie-.text: BRUSSELS — Europe’s three mainstream political groups must strike a deal to keep out the far right ahead of an election year that could reshape the EU, the head of the liberal Renew Europe group in the European Parliament told POLITICO. “I’m truly convinced that nobody can afford to let the coalition erode from a very practical point of view because this is the only way to deliver an ambitious and a stronger Europe for our citizens,” said Valérie Hayer, a close ally of French President Emmanuel Macron, adding that there’s “no other way.” Since the 2024 EU election shifted the Parliament to the right, the conservative European People’s Party — the largest in the assembly — has passed legislation with right-wing and far-right groups, angering its traditional liberal and social democratic allies. Hayer said Renew’s priority ahead of the next EU election, in 2029, is to rebuild the centrist alliance. Advertisement Advertisement Speaking by phone after a gathering of EU liberals ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday, Hayer said “we need a strong European platform from the center to deliver for Europeans” on issues such as competitiveness, defense, climate change and decarbonization, especially with major EU countries facing national elections, including Spain in November and Italy, France and Poland in 2027. “We should be prepared for this new cycle of elections.” To lock in the centrist majority, Hayer wants the three groups to strike a detailed coalition agreement. The EPP has largely voted with its centrist allies during the first half of the current term, but has occasionally turned to the right to pass legislation when disagreements with its traditional partners proved too difficult to bridge. Hayer said Renew would not back any candidate for Parliament president without first agreeing on a detailed coalition deal. “A majority needs a program before it needs a president, so we need a coalition agreement before any leadership agreement, and no coalition agreement would mean no leadership deal.” That could force the EPP to the negotiating table, as the conservatives want to get Roberta Metsola reelected for a third term in January. However, the EPP has in the past been reluctant to sign a detailed coalition agreement. Hayer and the leaders of the EPP (Manfred Weber) and Socialists and Democrats (Iratxe García) already signed a two-page agreement to work with each other after the 2024 EU election, but the EPP has nonetheless voted on laws with far-right groups. To prevent this, Hayer wants not only leaders but all “key members” of the groups, including vice-chairs, whips and coordinators, to negotiate and endorse the agreement. Advertisement Advertisement “I want us to be very concrete, I want a midterm agreement that binds us to delivery on the budget, on the IAA, for example, on EU Inc.” — referring to the Industrial Accelerator Act (a proposal to steer public procurement and subsidies toward European manufacturers) and a plan to give startups a single set of rules . She also wants the far right excluded from powerful posts in the Parliament, including vice-presidencies. Hayer said the centrist leaders had “already discussed” the agreement and expressed confidence it could advance. García has said she is ready to negotiate with the EPP to reach an agreement, although Weber hasn’t publicly commented on the idea. Hayer wants any candidate for Parliament president to be hands-on to ensure the center holds, because “you can’t say I’ve been elected and then I don’t care about the majority and the people who elected me.” Metsola says she needs to represent the entire hemicycle, but has voiced a preference for majorities built “from the center out.” Hayer also wants commissioners to “bring the groups together” before proposing new laws, in order that they have “a first discussion and first kind of agreement.” Asked if she trusted Weber to comply with any deal, Hayer said “ we are working together every day” and that any deal “should be done in a fair way and sincere way.” As for the socialists, she urged them to be “constructive in the negotiations.” Advertisement Advertisement
